glossary.Transfusion: Giving blood or a blood component, such as red cells, platelets or plasma, into a vein.
glossary.Packed red cells: Red blood cells with most of the plasma removed, the usual unit for anaemia.
glossary.Platelets: Small cell fragments that start clotting; stored at room temperature, so bacteria grow more easily.
glossary.Haemolytic: Caused by or involving destruction of red blood cells.
glossary.Haemolysis screen: Blood tests (Hb, LDH, bilirubin, haptoglobin, film, DAT) that look for red cell breakdown.
glossary.Cytokines: Small signalling proteins released by white cells that cause fever and inflammation.
glossary.Chills: Feeling cold and shivery, often as a temperature rises.
glossary.Back pain: Loin or lower back pain during transfusion, a warning of acute haemolysis.
glossary.Hodgkin's: Hodgkin lymphoma; these patients are at risk of transfusion-associated GvHD.
glossary.Immunosuppressed: Having a weakened immune system that cannot destroy donor white cells.
glossary.Jaundice: Yellow skin and eyes from raised bilirubin.
glossary.Bilirubin: A yellow breakdown product of haemoglobin; rises when red cells are destroyed.
glossary.U&Es: Urea and electrolytes: blood tests of kidney function and salts like potassium.
glossary.FBC: Full blood count: haemoglobin, white cells and platelets.
glossary.Hb: Haemoglobin, the oxygen-carrying protein in red cells.
glossary.Antiglobulin: An antibody against human antibodies, used in the DAT to show cells are coated.
glossary.Agglutination: Clumping of red cells when antibodies bind them, used in blood grouping.
glossary.Anti-A: An antibody against the A antigen; red cells clumping with it carry A antigen.
glossary.Group O: Blood with no A or B antigens, so O red cells can be given to anyone.
glossary.A-negative: Blood group A lacking the RhD antigen.
glossary.Compatibility: Whether donor blood can be safely given to a recipient without an immune reaction.
glossary.Corticosteroids: Anti-inflammatory steroid drugs such as hydrocortisone.
glossary.Bronchodilators: Drugs such as salbutamol that open narrowed airways.
glossary.Antihistamine: A drug blocking histamine receptors, used for itch and urticarial rash.
glossary.Paracetamol: A simple analgesic and antipyretic used for febrile reactions.
glossary.Urine output: Volume of urine produced; falls in shock and AKI.
glossary.Antigen: A molecule on a cell surface that an antibody can recognise.
glossary.Neutrophil: The commonest white cell; when activated it damages lung capillaries in TRALI.
glossary.Capillary leak: Fluid escaping from damaged small vessels into tissues.
glossary.Microvasculature: The smallest blood vessels: arterioles, capillaries and venules.
glossary.Volume overload: Too much fluid in the circulation for the heart to cope with.
glossary.Anti-IgA antibodies: Antibodies made by IgA-deficient people that attack IgA in donor plasma.
glossary.Plasma: The liquid part of blood, containing antibodies and clotting factors.
glossary.Hypertension: High blood pressure, here from fluid overload in TACO.
glossary.Cultures: Samples grown in the lab to identify bacteria, here from the patient and the blood bag.
glossary.Free haemoglobin: Haemoglobin released into plasma when red cells burst inside vessels.
glossary.Pre-formed: Already present before the transfusion, so the reaction is immediate.
glossary.Donor: The person who gave the blood.
